question.body: I am studying the unit on assistive technology. How do screen readers, Braille displays and voice input differ? Long phrases such as a refreshable Braille display also confuse me: which word names the device?
question.priorKnowledge: Can explain input and output functions and describe devices with adjectives.
question.interests: Making a fictional school website easier for different people to use.

personas.name: Maya
personas.role: Explainer: clear vocabulary and language patterns

personas.name: Leo
personas.role: Careful skeptic: tests assumptions and asks challenges

personas.name: Iris
personas.role: Connection maker: examples and communication practice

replies.body: **Unit focus: assistive technology and noun phrases.** The course title is retained here so you can match the unit. In your own writing, **people with disabilities** is a useful respectful default; follow an individual's preferred wording. Discuss a person's task and access needs rather than assuming everyone uses the same tool.

A **screen reader** presents interface content through speech or Braille. A **refreshable Braille display** provides tactile output. **Screen magnification** enlarges displayed content. **Speech recognition** supports spoken input. These tools solve different access problems and may be combined. Accessible text, meaningful labels and keyboard access help assistive technologies work effectively.
If a website includes a button showing a magnifying-glass icon, is the label magnifying glass enough? Also, can we decide which tool someone needs from a broad disability label alone?

Name the button's action: if it starts a search, **Search** is a more useful accessible name than a description of its shape. Ask what the person needs to do and how they prefer to interact. A disability label alone does not determine the best tool. A feature also needs usable content and controls; owning assistive hardware cannot fix every barrier on a poorly designed site.

A noun phrase has a **head** and may include words that describe it. In **a refreshable Braille display**, the head is **display**. In **speech recognition software**, the head is **software**. The earlier words narrow the meaning.

**Practice:** find the head in an alternative keyboard and a large on-screen button.

**Answers:** **keyboard** and **button**.

**Short email model:**

Hi Casey,
Our website should support keyboard navigation and meaningful control labels. A screen reader can present accessible text through speech or Braille, while speech recognition supports spoken input. We should ask users about their needs and test the actual tasks.

**Takeaway:** distinguish input from output, identify the head of long noun phrases, and describe access needs without making assumptions about individuals.
